incidents.title: Scammers use AI to impersonate immigration attorneys to dupe immigrants with fake legal services
incidents.summary:
Angel Leal, a South Florida immigration attorney with over 30 years of experience, has become the target of an artificial intelligence scam targeting vulnerable immigrants. Criminals have created hundreds of fake videos and social media profiles using AI-generated images of Leal to offer fraudulent immigration services, including false promises of US residency for $2,200. Leal discovered the scheme when potential clients began calling his office, and the situation has dramatically worsened in recent months. An anti-piracy company hired by his office has removed nearly 6,500 fake profiles, including 3,500 from TikTok, 2,400 from Facebook, and 544 from Instagram.

The scammers typically use social media videos directing victims to contact them via WhatsApp, where they send fake contracts and fake testimonials from supposed former clients. Leal warns consumers to be cautious of requests for payment through apps like Venmo, Zelle, or Cash App, emphasizing his office never requests payment over the phone. He plans to contact local and federal authorities to investigate the scams and urges immigrants to verify the identities of anyone offering legal services online.

incidents.title: ASIC warns scammers are using AI to spin vast webs of deception
incidents.summary:
# Summary

A fake online article falsely depicted Reserve Bank Governor Michele Bullock having a heated confrontation with ABC finance presenter Alan Kohler over an unlicensed cryptocurrency platform called Boulder Sparhaven. This fabricated interview never occurred but represents an increasingly common scam tactic. According to ASIC research released today, AI-generated deepfakes of celebrities and politicians are being used more frequently and convincingly to promote illegitimate investment schemes. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese tops the list of impersonated public figures, followed by other politicians and financial experts including Alan Kohler himself.

Last year, ASIC removed 19,400 scams, a 182 percent increase from the previous period. Notably, phishing scams jumped 279 percent with 5,476 removals, while fake investment platforms increased 151 percent to 7,051 takedowns. Scammers typically create elaborate webs of deception using fake news articles, websites, and advertisements before luring victims into providing personal details. ASIC advises consumers to verify Australian Financial Services license numbers through its public registers before investing. Alan Kohler has called for heavy fines against platforms hosting such content and the AI models generating it.

incidents.title: Sleep Staging Is Not Guesswork
incidents.summary:
# Summary

A lawsuit filed by Clarkson Law Firm in San Francisco alleges that Oura, the smart ring company valued at approximately eleven billion dollars, made false advertising claims about its sleep tracking capabilities. The suit, filed Thursday and seeking class action status, contends that Oura's rings priced at three hundred dollars and up cannot accurately measure sleep stages as advertised. The lawsuit claims the company's algorithms and sensors lack the ability to detect the physiological signals needed for accurate sleep measurement and instead rely on artificial intelligence generated guesses comparable to random chance, contradicting marketing statements such as claiming ninety-five percent sleep staging accuracy.

Oura responded by defending its science and research, stating that its rings estimate sleep stages using multiple physiological signals and have been validated against polysomnography, the gold standard for sleep measurement. However, industry experts noted that health trackers like Oura provide estimates rather than medical-grade diagnostics and that wearable technology has advanced faster than scientific research can validate. This lawsuit marks the second major legal action against Oura, following an ongoing class action alleging unauthorized collection of sensitive personal information for two years.

incidents.title: Caught in 4K: The Aurora Files
incidents.summary:
Gambit Security's Threat Intelligence team discovered that Aurora ransomware, active since April 2026, has developed a Linux variant targeting ESXi virtual machine environments. The group operates a data leak site and has targeted organizations across multiple countries. Researchers identified exposed infrastructure revealing that Aurora operators used Cursor Agent, an AI tool running Claude Sonnet, to conduct hands-on exploitation attacks against ten target organizations between mid-April and late May 2026. The ESXi ransomware variant encrypts virtual machine files while keeping the hypervisor bootable so victims can see ransom demands.

The attackers deployed custom tools including esxi_finder.py to scan networks for ESXi hosts and vCenter servers. When using Cursor Agent, operators provided credentials and tasked the AI with various exploitation activities like installing VPN clients, scanning internal networks, and attempting authentication relay attacks, while imposing strict restrictions against certain techniques like DCSync attacks or account lockouts. Researchers also identified a second Aurora cluster operating across eight victim organizations in Israel, Germany, Austria, Spain, the United States, and Argentina, using different tactics including SQL Server exploitation and data exfiltration to self-hosted storage.

incidents.title: A Pizza Hut franchisee is suing over a forced AI system it says wrecked deliveries
incidents.summary:
Chaac Pizza Northeast, which operates approximately 111 Pizza Hut restaurants across five northeastern states, filed a lawsuit in Texas Business Court on May 6 alleging that Pizza Hut's AI-powered delivery system called Dragontail caused over $100 million in damages. The franchisee claims the system created operational problems by giving DoorDash drivers real-time visibility into kitchen workflows, causing drivers to wait up to 15 minutes to batch multiple orders together rather than delivering pizzas immediately after they left the oven. The suit also alleges drivers could see tip amounts and payment methods, making them selective about which orders to accept.

Before Dragontail's 2024 rollout, Chaac maintained over 90% on-time deliveries and double-digit sales growth. After implementation, the franchisee experienced sharp performance declines, including year-over-year sales swinging from positive 10.19% to negative 9.78% in New York City. Chaac claims Pizza Hut failed to provide adequate training, refused support requests, and ignored worsening delivery metrics. The suit alleges Pizza Hut breached its franchise agreement by mandating continued use of the problematic software. Pizza Hut declined further comment and said it would respond through legal channels.

incidents.title: Inside the Fake Celebrity Podcast Scam Fooling Hollywood
incidents.summary:
Scammers are impersonating Terry Gross and other staff members of NPR's "Fresh Air" program to defraud potential interview guests. The fraudulent emails, which are highly personalized and reference the recipient's work, have targeted authors, entertainers, and other public figures. Recipients are eventually asked to pay fees for production costs, though WHYY has stated it never charges guests for interviews. One victim, history professor Jennifer Black from Misericordia University, initially believed the invitation was legitimate before suspecting artificial intelligence was involved and noticing a request for $250.

WHYY, NPR, and law enforcement are investigating the scam, which has also targeted other celebrities including comedians Nikki Glaser and Amy Poehler. Cybersecurity expert Aunshul Rege notes that AI has made scams more convincing and personalized than traditional fraud attempts. Red flags include requests for payment, the use of Gmail addresses, and the unusual situation of a famous host personally handling logistics. WHYY recommends verifying any interview requests through legitimate contact channels rather than responding to suspicious emails.

incidents.title: Fake US thinktank set up and funded by Israel sought to game AI for propaganda
incidents.summary:
# Summary

A fake American research institute called the Hanover Institute, funded by the Israeli government, published over 560,000 words across 124 reports in nine days to manipulate artificial intelligence chatbots into favoring pro-Israel arguments. The institute, which has no legal entity status or physical address, presented one-sided material on topics including Palestinian torture, Israeli war crimes, and Gaza starvation as neutral research. The operation was coordinated through Israeli advertising agency LaPam and European firm Havas Media, with contracts routed through American companies including Piro Inc, which filed the disclosure required under the Foreign Agents Registration Act.

The effort is part of a broader, multi-million dollar campaign to influence AI training data and chatbot responses about Israel. The Guardian found that the institute's reports were designed using generative engine optimization techniques to appear credible to AI systems. However, Israeli officials have expressed frustration that the expensive public diplomacy campaign has failed to improve Israel's declining support among American voters, with polls showing decreased sympathy for Israel and increased concerns about military actions in Gaza, particularly among younger Americans and Democrats.

incidents.title: Round Hill is suing Suno and Anthropic for up to $1B apiece. It isn’t looking to settle.
incidents.summary:
Major record labels, including Universal Music Group, Sony Music, Warner Music, Capitol Records, and Atlantic Records, have filed lawsuits against Udio and Suno, two popular AI music generators. The labels accuse these companies of scraping massive amounts of copyrighted music without permission to train their models and of directly reproducing sections of famous songs in their AI-generated outputs. The record labels submitted a lengthy list of thousands of copyrighted works they claim were used for training, featuring catalogs from artists like The Beatles, Michael Jackson, Frank Sinatra, and many others.

To support their claims, the record labels tested both AI music generators using specific prompts and demonstrated that they could repeatedly recreate versions of famous copyrighted songs. For example, they generated AI music that closely mimicked Chuck Berry's "Johnny B. Goode" and created a near-identical version of Mariah Carey's "All I Want for Christmas Is You." The lawsuits were filed in New York against Udio and in Massachusetts against Suno, setting up a significant court battle over how generative AI services should handle copyrighted material across music, art, video, and text.

# Summary

Universal Music Group and AI music startup Udio have reached a settlement, ending a lawsuit that accused Udio of using copyrighted music to train its artificial intelligence system. UMG, along with Sony Music and Warner Music Group, had sued Udio for allegedly creating songs similar to popular hits without permission or compensation, including a track resembling The Temptations' "My Girl." Under the agreement, Udio will launch a new platform next year trained only on authorized and licensed music, allowing users to create, customize, and share songs. The financial terms were not disclosed.

Udio, founded in 2024 by former Google DeepMind employees and backed by investors including musician will.i.am and venture capital firm Andreessen Horowitz, will compensate artists who opt into the new platform. The settlement marks Udio's first music licensing deal with a major label. Meanwhile, UMG also announced a partnership with Stability AI to develop music creation tools for artists and producers. Millions of users have accessed Udio since its launch, with approximately 128,000 app downloads since May.

incidents.title: AI Hallucinations in State Farm Insurance Outside Lawyers' Filings
incidents.summary:
State Farm's defense lawyers apologized after being caught using artificial intelligence that generated fake legal cases, nonexistent quotes, and false holdings in court filings for a lawsuit involving a Los Angeles homeowner. The homeowner, Fa'alagilagi Meni-Siliga, sued State Farm and others after a 2020 fire left her Carson home uninhabitable, followed by storm damage and delayed repairs. She claims the delays and incomplete work led her family to drain their savings, declare bankruptcy, and lose their home to foreclosure. State Farm argued she failed to file within a year and blamed negligence by the plaintiff and contractors.

Lawyer Jacquelene Robinson admitted using an AI tool called Irys to help prepare motions, believing it performed accuracy checks when it did not. She confirmed seven case citations across eight filings did not exist, along with incorrect case titles and fabricated quotes. Her supervising attorney, Kenneth Katel, took responsibility despite not knowing AI was used. The case goes to trial in October. This incident reflects a broader trend, with 41 percent of law firms now using generative AI, and a database tracking 1,922 documented cases of legal AI hallucinations worldwide.

stories.Headline: Electoral court sets new standards for AI deepfakes
stories.Summary:
Brazil's highest electoral court established new guidelines for identifying artificial intelligence-generated deepfakes in political content ahead of October elections. The ruling came from a case involving opposition candidate Senator Flávio Bolsonaro, who displayed AI-created images of his imprisoned father, former President Jair Bolsonaro, at his party's convention in July. The deepfake showed the former president endorsing his son's campaign against current President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva. Jair Bolsonaro is serving a 27-year prison sentence for attempting to lead a coup.

The court voted 4-3 to not punish Senator Bolsonaro, determining the deepfake was shown at a private party event rather than a public political advertisement. However, the court voted 5-2 to formally define what constitutes a deepfake in political advertising as synthetic content created or altered using artificial intelligence technology that realistically reproduces a person's image, voice, or speech. These standards will apply to thousands of campaign ads broadcasters must air before the October 4 election, during 14 minutes of daily airtime designated for political commercials.

stories.Headline: NYC, the nation's largest school district, bans AI for students through 8th grade - ABC News - Breaking News, Latest News and Videos
stories.Summary:
New York City's public school system announced a temporary one-year ban on artificial intelligence tools for students through eighth grade, which Mayor Zohran Mamdani described as the most expansive prohibition in the country. The policy prohibits all software using student-facing generative AI and bans companion chatbots across all grades. Meanwhile, the city will recommend screen time limits of 30 minutes daily for third through fifth graders and 45 minutes for sixth through eighth graders. Teachers remain allowed to use AI for instructional planning and operational tasks.

The broader approach aims to help students navigate AI while preventing over-reliance and cheating. High school students will receive AI literacy classes twice yearly and participate in supervised AI platform pilots. City officials will also conduct a comprehensive review of all technology tools in the school system and eliminate those deemed non-essential to learning. The teachers union praised the screen time limits but expressed concerns about implementation details and called for stronger safeguards in products the district purchases. Students are scheduled to return to classrooms the following week.

stories.Headline: Nvidia's $12.9B Hugging Face Deal Tests AI Platform Neutrality
stories.Summary:
Nvidia is acquiring Hugging Face, a major artificial intelligence model repository, for $12.9 billion. The deal will provide Hugging Face with significantly increased computing power and resources that company leadership says are necessary for expansion. However, the acquisition raises concerns about whether Hugging Face can maintain its neutrality as an open-source alternative to proprietary artificial intelligence platforms, given that Nvidia manufactures the GPU hardware that powers these systems.

Hugging Face co-founder and CEO Clement Delangue stated that the company requires Nvidia's support and additional computing resources to scale operations effectively. Industry observers worry that Nvidia's ownership could create conflicts of interest regarding the infrastructure that customers use to build artificial intelligence systems on Hugging Face's platform. The acquisition marks a significant consolidation in the artificial intelligence industry between a major hardware provider and a prominent software platform.

stories.Headline: Lawmakers propose oversight for state, local agencies using AI - Yahoo
stories.Summary:
Nevada lawmakers are proposing legislation to establish basic standards for how state and local government agencies use artificial intelligence. Democratic state Senator Dina Neal recommended the committee pursue this action due to concerns about the lack of oversight and potential risks associated with integrating AI systems without legal requirements. The proposed legislation would require transparency around AI use and prevent bias in automated decision-making. Several Nevada agencies, including the Department of Employment, Training, and Rehabilitation and the Department of Motor Vehicles, have already implemented AI systems. Some people have reportedly been denied benefits and unable to speak with a human during appeals processes.

The nine bill draft requests, including the AI oversight proposal, were approved at an August 27 interim Government Affairs Committee meeting. The legislation will be considered during the 2027 Legislative Session beginning February 1. State Senator Edgar Flores emphasized the importance of ensuring humans ultimately make important decisions rather than relying solely on automated systems. Senator Neal said the state needs to audit agencies and determine how many errors have occurred where human response was needed but did not happen. Lawmakers anticipate facing resistance from state and local agencies when the bill is discussed.

stories.Headline: US government backs OpenAI in New York Times lawsuit - Kuwait Times
stories.Summary:
The Trump administration filed a legal document supporting OpenAI in its copyright dispute with the New York Times. The Justice Department argued that training artificial intelligence models on copyrighted articles qualifies as "exceedingly transformative" and is protected under fair use law. Officials contended that restricting such AI development would harm American economic growth and national security competitiveness. The administration claimed that limiting AI training would create unfair barriers favoring established media companies.

The New York Times sued OpenAI and Microsoft in late 2023, claiming the companies used millions of its articles to train ChatGPT without permission or compensation. A spokesman for the newspaper criticized the Justice Department for siding with major tech companies against American creators. The legal ruling could significantly impact ongoing copyright disputes in the AI industry, as publishers, musicians, and artists pursue similar claims about unauthorized use of their content for AI development.

stories.Headline: LAUSD adopts moratorium on student AI use, another big move to limit classroom computer time - Los Angeles Times
stories.Summary:
The Los Angeles Unified School District has implemented a moratorium on student use of generative artificial intelligence on school devices for the current school year. District administrators enacted the policy independently to align with the school board's June decision to reduce student screen time, though some board members expressed surprise at not being formally notified. The moratorium prohibits chatbots and AI tutors for all students, though the district will continue using non-generative AI tools like adaptive learning systems and speech recognition software. Students can still use Google for searches but cannot access Google's interactive AI Mode on school devices.

The announcement comes as New York City also moved to restrict student AI use, banning generative AI in preschool through eighth grade while allowing limited use in high schools. Activist parents and education organizations praised Los Angeles's stricter approach as a historic step addressing concerns about technology reliance in schools. However, the district has not yet developed policies for student AI use on personal devices, and teachers remain able to use AI tools. Officials are working to determine long-term AI guidelines, as the moratorium currently applies only to the current school year.
